name: Romaine Lettuce
portion: A cup or two of leaves per day
notes: A solid everyday leafy green. Skip iceberg-type lettuce in favor of darker, leafier varieties.

name: Bell Pepper
portion: A few slices, 3-4 times a week
notes: Very high in vitamin C, which guinea pigs can't produce on their own. Red peppers have the most.

name: Cucumber
portion: A few slices per day
notes: Mostly water, so it's more of a hydrating treat than a nutrition source.

name: Cilantro
portion: A small handful a few times a week
notes: Most guinea pigs love it, and it's easy on digestion.

name: Parsley
portion: A small handful, 2-3 times a week
notes: Good vitamin C source, but fairly high in calcium, so it shouldn't be a daily staple.

name: Carrot
portion: A few thin slices, a couple times a week
notes: Guinea pigs love it, but it's higher in sugar than most safe vegetables.

name: Celery
portion: A stalk or two, chopped small
notes: Chop it into short pieces first — the long strings can be a minor choking risk.

name: Zucchini
portion: A few slices a few times a week
notes: Skin and all is fine, just wash it first.

name: Kale
portion: A small handful, once or twice a week
notes: Nutritious but high in calcium and oxalates, which can contribute to bladder stones if overdone.

name: Broccoli
portion: A small floret a couple times a week
notes: Fine in small amounts, but too much can cause gas.

name: Tomato
portion: A few small pieces, 2-3 times a week
notes: Only the ripe flesh — the green stems and leaves are toxic and should never be given.

name: Blueberries
portion: A couple berries, once or twice a week
notes: Tasty treat, but sugar content means it shouldn't be an everyday food.

name: Strawberries
portion: One small berry, once or twice a week
notes: Same idea as blueberries — a treat, not a staple, because of the sugar.

name: Apple
portion: A small slice, once or twice a week
notes: Remove the seeds first. Sugar content means small portions only.

name: Banana
portion: A thin slice, once a week at most
notes: One of the higher-sugar fruits guinea pigs are commonly given — keep it occasional.

name: Orange
portion: A small segment, once a week
notes: Good vitamin C, but the acidity can bother some guinea pigs' mouths if given too often.

name: Basil
portion: A few leaves, a few times a week
notes: Safe and generally well tolerated.

name: Dandelion Greens
portion: A small handful a few times a week
notes: Only from areas you know haven't been treated with pesticides.

name: Timothy Hay
portion: Unlimited, available at all times
notes: Should make up the bulk of a guinea pig's diet — good for digestion and keeps their teeth worn down.

name: Iceberg Lettuce
portion: Best avoided or given only occasionally
notes: Not toxic, but mostly water with little nutritional value, and can cause loose stools in larger amounts.

name: Chocolate
portion: Never
notes: Contains theobromine, which is toxic to guinea pigs.

name: Avocado
portion: Never
notes: Contains persin, which is toxic to guinea pigs.

name: Onion
portion: Never
notes: Can damage red blood cells and cause anemia.

name: Garlic
portion: Never
notes: Same risk as onion — avoid entirely.

name: Rhubarb
portion: Never
notes: High in oxalic acid, especially the leaves — toxic to guinea pigs.

name: Raw Potato
portion: Never
notes: Contains solanine, which is toxic. This includes any green-tinged potato.

name: Nuts and Seeds
portion: Never
notes: Too high in fat for a guinea pig's digestive system, and a choking hazard.

name: Dairy Products
portion: Never
notes: Guinea pigs are herbivores and can't digest dairy properly.
